Today through Thursday: The Inland NW will be situated in a 
southerly flow with a trough of low pressure off the Pacific 
Coast. A front remains stalled near the eastern CWA and a couple 
upper shortwaves will be riding north into the area through 
Wednesday, before the offshore trough makes a run at pushing 
farther inland. With that latter detail, models are still not in 
full agreement or consistency on how that looks. Around 55 
percent of the ensembles bring the trough in, 28 percent hold it 
offshore and 17 percent are somewhere in the middle. Overall, 
this pattern will lead to some expansion of shower and 
thunderstorm chances, but confidence in details remains low to 
fair and they would tend to be on the drier side.

First today one shortwave will ride north along the boundary over
the southeast, bringing broader middle to upper clouds, with some
cumulus development too. Models diverge some with the 
precipitation potential, but I think the potential has not been 
high enough in the NBM as of late because most recent guidance has
trended to show more returns coming over southeast WA through the
ID Panhandle. There is even less confidence in t-storms 
potential. The best agreement is near the far southeastern CWA. 
Some outlying models show shower and even t-storm chances as far 
west the Spokane area and Upper Columbia Basin, but confidence is 
lower and looking at recent sounding data, the drier atmosphere 
would tend to limit precipitation away from the deeper southeast 
moisture. So the main potential stays painted over that SE WA/ID 
area. I increased PoPs over the NBM, to expand the risk further on
to the Palouse and C'dA area. This potential starts early this 
morning in the south and expands northeastward through mid to late
morning to afternoon, before waning. Some sprinkles cannot be 
ruled out around Spokane, the Upper Columbia Basin and northeast 
mountains today.

Chances expand out again again during the day Wednesday, with the
higher focus around the mountain zones. Embedded t-storms will be
possible in the afternoon and early evening too. Again we will 
have to keep an eye out for outlying model solutions that paint 
some risk around the basin. As we head into Thursday and that 
trough starts to edge inland per most guidance, the risk of 
showers and embedded t-storms expands over a broader area. Right 
now guidance is favoring the Cascades and western basin into the 
northern mountains with the highest risk in the southerly flow and
proximity to the trough axis. However if that trough shifts 
further inland, the shower/t-storm threat would be a bit broader
and models did trend a bit higher in this period. 

Regardless of the overall precipitation chances, models are not 
showing a lot of QPF; meaning any t-storms would tend to be on the
drier side. So we will have to monitor that for fire concerns. At
this point I am not expecting a lot, but there is still some 
disagreement. Gusty outflow winds, lightning and the risk for fire
starts remains the main impacts we will be monitoring. 

Overall winds are forecast to be occasionally breezy near the 
Cascades to western basin each afternoon, but nothing too strong. 
There may be some outflow gusts from showers today near eastern 
WA. Other locally stronger winds are forecast near the Okanogan 
Valley/Waterville Plateau this afternoon and with RH values in the
teens; so this will mean some elevated fire conditions. By later 
Thursday more guidance shows the trough shifting far enough east 
to start to turn the flow westerly and this would also lead to 
some increased winds near the Cascade gaps and western basin. 
Again the precise timing of this will impact the strength, as if 
they westerly push coincides with the drainage winds there could 
be local enhancements. Afternoon relative humidity values bottom 
out in the teens to lows, save for near the southeast CWA and ID 
today where minimum RH values are 30s and 40s. With the breezy, 
dry conditions some elevated fire conditions are forecast near the
lee Cascade zones and Okanogan Valley to Waterville Plateau the 
next couple days.

Temperatures are expected to remain warm to hot, with widespread 
highs in the 90s. Some upper 80s are possible toward the southeast
CWA where more clouds and the limited shower chances could hold 
things back. Thursday as the potential to be the warmest day of 
the week, but there is still a large spread in the 25 to 75 
percentile at over a 10 degree difference. This is owing to the 
widespread in the solution of how that offshore trough moves 
inland. On average, though, the temperatures are forecast to 
remain hot. Widespread moderate HeatRisk is in the forecast.

Friday to Monday: models continue to show some spread in the 
overall set-up. However ensembles generally seem to trend trough 
weaker with a ridge amplifying over the region heading into the
